metaDescription: Columbia, SC renovation contractor for investors: Shandon bungalows, Olympia mill houses and Midlands ranches priced free before you buy, with draws after work.
intro: Columbia's heat is part of every renovation conversation here. Long, punishing summers decide how hard an HVAC system works, how fast a vacant house grows mold and how quickly termites move through framing, and the city's location on the fall line gives it sandy soil in some neighborhoods and red clay in others. On top of that sits a housing stock built in layers: early twentieth-century bungalows in Shandon, Cottontown and Elmwood Park, mill houses in Olympia and Granby, post-war ranches in Rosewood, Eau Claire and Dentsville, and suburban subdivisions spreading toward Irmo, Lexington and Blythewood. Genstone Construction renovates those houses for investors, lenders and servicers across the Midlands. We're headquartered in Romeoville, Illinois, and in Columbia we coordinate vetted, licensed South Carolina contractors managed by a designated Genstone field manager. Every project starts with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that estimates repairs and tests the after-repair value before you commit. You then get an itemized scope with a draw schedule paid against completed work, no upfront payment and a one-year workmanship warranty once you approve the finished house.
housingStock:
Columbia's oldest residential neighborhoods ring downtown and the University of South Carolina. Elmwood Park, Cottontown and the Bellevue area north of downtown hold Victorian and Craftsman houses from the 1890s through the 1930s, many on brick piers with crawlspaces, heart pine floors, plaster walls and deep porches. Waverly, east of downtown, is one of the city's historic African American neighborhoods, with houses from the same era. Shandon, Wales Garden, Earlewood and Melrose Heights filled in during the 1910s through the 1940s with bungalows, cottages and period revival houses, often on raised crawlspaces with wood siding or brick veneer.

The textile mills along the Congaree River left Olympia and Granby, where rows of one- and two-story frame mill houses still stand on brick piers. Many have been renovated as the area attracted students and young buyers, but plenty remain in original condition with board walls, small rooms and dated additions.

After World War II, Rosewood, Eau Claire, Hollywood-Rose Hill and North Columbia saw waves of small brick and frame houses, followed by brick ranches in Dentsville, St. Andrews and the areas around Fort Jackson in the 1950s through the 1970s. The 1980s and later brought suburban growth to Harbison, Irmo, Lexington, Northeast Columbia and Blythewood, with vinyl and brick two-stories and ranches on slabs and crawlspaces.

For investors, each layer has a predictable budget profile. Bungalows and mill houses spend on piers, floor framing, termite damage, wiring and plumbing. Post-war ranches spend on HVAC, ductwork, electrical service, bathrooms and kitchens. Newer suburban houses mainly need roofs, HVAC equipment, water heaters and windows as original components age, along with polybutylene replacement in some 1980s and 1990s homes. Enclosed porches and rear additions built over the decades are common in every older neighborhood, and they're often where the worst framing and roofing problems hide.

commonIssues.title: Termite damage in crawlspaces and sills
commonIssues.body: Subterranean termites are active across the Midlands year-round, and Columbia's warm, humid climate gives them a long working season. Older houses on brick piers, especially in Olympia, Cottontown, Shandon and Waverly, often have damaged sills, floor joists and porch framing, and slab houses can have hidden damage in walls and door frames. Buyers' lenders usually require a clean wood-destroying insect report, known in South Carolina as a CL-100. A Columbia rehab budget should include treatment and repair, sized after a proper inspection.

commonIssues.title: HVAC strain and ductwork
commonIssues.body: Columbia's summers push air conditioning to its limits, and undersized or aging systems struggle to keep houses comfortable. Ductwork in crawlspaces and attics is often leaky, crushed or poorly insulated, which wastes much of what a new unit produces. Replacing equipment without addressing ducts leaves tenants and buyers unhappy. We evaluate the system as a whole and price proper sizing, sealed or replaced ducts and correct return air, since comfort complaints are one of the biggest sources of rental calls in the Midlands.

commonIssues.title: Moisture and mold in crawlspaces
commonIssues.body: Humid air entering vented crawlspaces condenses on cool ductwork and floor framing, and poor drainage adds water from below. The result is mold on joists, sagging insulation, rusted duct boots and cupped floors. The issue is common in Shandon, Rosewood and other neighborhoods with older crawlspace houses. The fix usually combines exterior drainage, a proper vapor barrier, sealed ducts and sometimes encapsulation or dehumidification, depending on the property and exit plan.

commonIssues.title: Flood history near Gills Creek and the rivers
commonIssues.body: The October 2015 flood hit Columbia hard, particularly along Gills Creek and the neighborhoods near Forest Acres and southeast Columbia, and some properties never received full repairs. Signs include replaced lower drywall, warped subfloors, mold in crawlspaces and rusted mechanical equipment. Houses near the Congaree, Broad and Saluda rivers and their tributaries carry similar risk. Check flood zone status and history before buying, since both affect insurance cost, repairs and the after-repair value.

commonIssues.title: Old wiring, plumbing and lead
commonIssues.body: Columbia's pre-1950 houses often contain knob-and-tube wiring, early ungrounded circuits, galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains, while some 1980s and 1990s houses have polybutylene plumbing. Most houses built before 1978 have lead paint somewhere, and mid-century materials like floor tile and duct wrap can contain asbestos. A full systems assessment is part of every Columbia Pre-Offer Rehab Review because these items are expensive and almost always flagged by buyer inspectors and insurers.

investorMarket:
Columbia's investor market runs on three anchors: the University of South Carolina, Fort Jackson and state government. USC creates steady demand for rentals in the neighborhoods around campus, including Shandon, Rosewood, Olympia, Granby and the Five Points area, where single-family houses and small multifamily properties rent to students and young professionals. Fort Jackson, the Army's largest basic training installation, supports rentals for military personnel and civilian staff, particularly in Dentsville and northeast Columbia. State government, hospitals and the insurance industry support a broad base of working renters.

Flips perform well in neighborhoods where renovated houses have already set the price, such as Shandon, Rosewood, Melrose Heights, Wales Garden, Earlewood and parts of Cottontown and Elmwood Park. Buyers there want character along with modern systems. Rental and BRRRR investors often target post-war ranches in North Columbia, Eau Claire, Dentsville and St. Andrews, as well as nearby West Columbia and Cayce, where purchase prices leave room for full renovation.

Small multifamily includes duplexes and small buildings near USC and Five Points, some divided houses in older neighborhoods and 1970s and 1980s duplexes and fourplexes across the suburbs. REO properties appear across the city, and flood-affected houses near Gills Creek occasionally surface with damage that requires careful scoping.
permits:
The City of Columbia's building inspections staff, part of its planning and development services, issue building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits and perform inspections inside the city limits. Richland County Building Codes and Inspections handles unincorporated Richland County, and Lexington County and towns like West Columbia, Cayce and Forest Acres run their own departments, so the jurisdiction depends on the address. Permits are needed for structural repairs, foundation and pier work, wall removals, additions, new or relocated plumbing and electrical, HVAC replacements, water heaters, roofing beyond minor repairs and decks. South Carolina enforces statewide building codes adopted by the state Building Codes Council, and residential contractors must be licensed or registered through the South Carolina Residential Builders Commission.

Columbia protects several historic and architectural conservation districts, including Elmwood Park, Cottontown, Waverly and Wales Garden, where exterior changes are reviewed by the city's Design/Development Review Commission or its staff. Floodplain rules apply to properties in FEMA flood hazard areas. Genstone's field manager handles permit applications, design review, inspections and lien waivers from every trade.
climate: Columbia's climate is hot and humid, with summers that rank among the hottest in the Southeast. Long stretches of high heat put enormous load on HVAC systems, drive humidity into crawlspaces and accelerate mold in vacant houses. Afternoon thunderstorms bring heavy rain that tests gutters, grading and roofs, and tropical systems occasionally bring wind and flooding inland, as the 2015 flood showed. Winters are short and generally mild, with occasional freezes and rare ice or snow, so freeze damage is uncommon but not impossible in vacant houses. Termites stay active much of the year. For scheduling, roofing, painting and exterior work go most smoothly in spring and fall, while summer is better suited to interior work in conditioned spaces. Crews in Columbia often start early in summer to avoid the worst afternoon heat.

faqs.q: Does Genstone have an office in Columbia?
faqs.a: No. Genstone Construction is headquartered in Romeoville, Illinois, and our Columbia work is done through a network of vetted, licensed and insured South Carolina contractors. Each project has a designated Genstone field manager who oversees scope, schedule, permits and inspections. Photos and milestones are shared throughout, which helps out-of-state investors and institutional clients manage Columbia renovations without being on site.

faqs.a: We focus on the items that drive budgets in Columbia: termite damage and the likely CL-100 outcome, HVAC and ductwork condition, crawlspace moisture, flood zone and flood history, wiring and plumbing age and whether the house is in a protected historic or architectural conservation district. We estimate the repair cost, check the after-repair value against nearby sales and tell you whether the numbers support your offer before you commit capital.

faqs.a: Yes. Our Columbia-area work covers the Midlands, including West Columbia, Cayce, Irmo, Lexington, Forest Acres, Blythewood and Chapin. Each jurisdiction issues its own permits and has its own zoning rules, and we work with the correct office for every property. Our process stays the same: free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, line-item estimate with a draw schedule, a designated field manager and payment tied to completed work.

faqs.a: No payment is required before work starts. Your estimate includes a draw schedule, and each draw is released after the matching work is completed and documented with photos and, where relevant, passed inspections. The last payment is held until the house is complete and you've signed off. fix-flip.metaDescription: Fix and flip contractor in Columbia, SC: Shandon and Rosewood bungalows, Olympia mill houses and Midlands ranches renovated to local comps, draws after work.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Columbia
fix-flip.intro: Columbia buyers judge a flip in two ways: what they see on the tour and what the CL-100 termite letter and home inspection say afterward. In Shandon, Rosewood and Melrose Heights, the tour matters a great deal, because buyers compare your house against well-renovated neighbors. On every Columbia flip, though, the paperwork can undo a sale if termite damage, HVAC problems or old wiring were missed. Genstone Construction scopes Columbia flips against renovated sales near your property and prices the hidden items first. Our estimates list labor and materials line by line, include a draw schedule and often compare two finish levels with separate after-repair values. A designated field manager runs the work with licensed South Carolina trades and documents everything for your listing agent.

sections.h2: Shandon, Rosewood and Melrose Heights buyers
sections.body:
The neighborhoods southeast of downtown, including Shandon, Rosewood, Melrose Heights, Wales Garden and Earlewood on the north side, attract buyers who want older houses close to USC, Five Points and downtown. Many are young professionals, hospital and government employees and faculty, and they're comparing your flip against carefully renovated bungalows on the same street. A renovation there should refinish heart pine or oak floors, keep original trim and doors where possible, restore porches and preserve the character that drew buyers to the neighborhood.

Behind the walls, those buyers expect modern systems: new wiring and panel, PEX supply lines, a properly sized heat pump with sealed ductwork, and a dry, clean crawlspace. Kitchens often need to be reworked for better flow, and adding a second bathroom is frequently what makes a two-bedroom bungalow competitive. In protected districts like Wales Garden or Cottontown, exterior changes need design review. We price finish options against neighborhood comps so you can match the scope to the street rather than to a generic package.

sections.h2: Mill houses in Olympia and Granby
sections.body:
Olympia and Granby, the mill villages near the Congaree River and USC, have become popular with students, young buyers and investors. Their frame mill houses are small, with simple floor plans, brick pier foundations and board walls that are often covered by later materials. Many have been renovated, which gives appraisers good comps, but plenty remain in original or poorly updated condition.

Renovating a mill house starts below the floor. Piers frequently need rebuilding, sills and joists are often damaged by termites and moisture, and floors may slope noticeably. Wiring and plumbing are usually original or patched and need full replacement. Insulation and air sealing make a dramatic difference in comfort and utility costs in Columbia's heat. Once the structure and systems are sound, finishes should match the renovated houses nearby, which typically means refinished floors, a functional kitchen, an updated bath and a porch that suits the house. We price the structural work up front so it doesn't surprise you after demolition.

sections.h2: Termites, heat and the inspection on Columbia flips
sections.body:
Most Columbia flips that run into trouble under contract do so because of the termite letter or the inspection report. Buyers' lenders typically require a CL-100 showing no active infestation and documenting any damage, and inspectors look closely at HVAC performance, ductwork, crawlspace moisture, roof condition and electrical safety.

We handle those items before finishes. That means termite treatment and framing repairs with documentation, a heat pump sized for the house with sealed or replaced ducts, a vapor barrier and drainage correction in the crawlspace, a panel upgrade and rewiring where needed, and a roof with remaining life. We schedule exterior work for spring and fall when possible and keep interior work moving through the summer. Draws are tied to completed work, and photos and inspection results are shared throughout. Financing can come from Genstone Financial's fix-and-flip loans or credit lines, or from the lender you already use. The permit and inspection records become part of the package your listing agent can share.

faqs.q: What is a CL-100 and why does it matter for Columbia flips?
faqs.a: The CL-100 is South Carolina's official wood-infestation report, completed by a licensed pest control company. Most lenders require one before closing, and it notes active infestation and visible damage. A flip with untreated termites or unrepaired damage may face repair demands or a canceled sale. We include treatment and framing repairs in the scope when needed, so the house is ready for a clean report before listing.

faqs.q: Is it worth flipping a mill house in Olympia?
faqs.a: It can be, especially where renovated mill houses nearby have set a strong resale benchmark. The main risk is underestimating foundation and framing work, since piers, sills and joists often need repair. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review looks under the house before you commit so the structural budget is known. Once the house is standing straight, its modest size keeps the finish budget in check.

faqs.q: Do you work on flips in West Columbia and Cayce?
faqs.a: Yes. We work across the Midlands, including West Columbia, Cayce, Lexington, Irmo and Forest Acres. Each has its own permitting office and zoning rules, and we handle permits through the correct jurisdiction. Our process stays the same everywhere: free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, line-item estimate with draw schedule, designated field manager and payment tied to completed work. Lexington County buyers often compare against newer construction nearby, so finish expectations there can run a little higher than in older parts of the city.

brrrr.intro: Columbia's rental demand rests on a diverse base: University of South Carolina students and staff, Fort Jackson personnel, state government employees and hospital workers. That breadth helps BRRRR investors, because rental demand doesn't depend on any one employer, and purchase prices on post-war ranches in many neighborhoods still leave room for full renovations. Genstone Construction renovates BRRRR properties across Columbia and the Midlands to reach the refinance appraisal and hold up to years of tenants in a hot, humid climate. Our estimators build the scope from renovated comps, a designated field manager runs the job with licensed South Carolina trades, and every repair is documented for your refinance lender and appraiser.

sections.body:
BRRRR deals in Columbia typically come from neighborhoods with moderate purchase prices and recent renovated sales. North Columbia, Eau Claire, Hollywood-Rose Hill, Dentsville and St. Andrews have large inventories of post-war ranches and small brick houses that fit the model. West Columbia and Cayce across the river offer similar stock. Houses near USC can work as rentals but often trade at prices better suited to flips or student-focused strategies. Neighborhoods near Fort Jackson attract military tenants and civilian staff.

The Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps you test each deal. We estimate the full renovation, compare the result with renovated sales nearby and show you whether the refinance is likely to return your capital. Columbia-specific risks include termite damage that needs structural repair, crawlspace moisture and mold, undersized or failing HVAC, and flood history near Gills Creek and the rivers. Properties in flood zones also carry insurance costs that affect DSCR calculations, so we flag that early.

sections.h2: Renovating for the Columbia refinance appraisal
sections.body:
Appraisers in Richland and Lexington counties compare your rental against renovated sales nearby and rate its condition and quality. A house with a renovated kitchen and baths, new flooring, a newer heat pump with sealed ducts, an updated electrical panel and a recent roof earns a stronger rating than one with partial updates. Visible problems such as termite damage, water stains, an old panel or a musty crawlspace can pull down the rating.

Our Columbia scopes go after exactly those weak spots. For Columbia ranches, that usually includes HVAC replacement with ductwork, roof replacement when needed, panel upgrade, PEX supply lines, crawlspace vapor barrier and drainage, termite treatment and repair, kitchen and bath renovation and durable flooring. We provide an appraisal package with permit records, final inspections, the CL-100, an improvement list and before-and-after photos, so the appraiser has documented evidence of what was done behind walls and under floors. Bringing the termite letter to the appraisal visit helps, because an appraiser who sees old damage under the house will want proof it was repaired.

Columbia's heat and humidity should drive material choices in a rental. HVAC comes first: a properly sized heat pump with sealed ducts and good return air keeps tenants comfortable and reduces service calls during long summers. Programmable thermostats and accessible filter locations help tenants run the system properly. Attic insulation and ventilation reduce the load further.

Inside, luxury vinyl plank handles humidity and pets, while refinished hardwood works in older ranches where it's sound. Bathrooms need exterior-vented fans and surrounds that don't leak at seams, since mold grows quickly in this climate. Under the house, a vapor barrier and sealed ducts reduce moisture problems. Outside, gutters, downspout extensions and grading keep water away from the foundation, which also makes the house less inviting to termites. A renewable termite bond protects the framing over time. These choices cost more up front and less over the years you hold the property. In older Midlands ranches, adding a return in the hallway alone often fixes the uneven cooling tenants complain about.

faqs.q: Do Fort Jackson tenants affect BRRRR planning in Columbia?
faqs.a: They can. Military tenants and civilian staff provide steady demand in neighborhoods near the base, but military moves can shorten tenancies. Durable materials and fast turns matter more in those areas. We design rental renovations so turns can be completed quickly with standard materials, which reduces vacancy when tenants leave on short notice. Houses in Dentsville and northeast Columbia that sit within a short drive of the post gates tend to see the most military interest. Many of those tenants view properties remotely, so clean listing photos and documented upgrades help as well.

faqs.q: Are student rentals near USC good BRRRR properties?
faqs.a: They can be, but they need tougher materials and more bedrooms, and some lenders treat student-oriented rentals differently for DSCR loans. Columbia also has zoning limits on unrelated occupants in some areas, so check before planning bedroom additions. Renovations focus on hard-surface flooring, solid doors and mechanical systems that handle heavy use. Properties in Olympia and Granby that rent by the bedroom also see more wear on bathrooms and kitchens, so we typically put the budget there first.

faqs.q: Can Genstone coordinate the DSCR refinance?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial, a Genstone company, lends DSCR rental money along with fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit. Using them is optional. With any lender, we provide the itemized scope, permit records, inspection results, CL-100 and photos needed for the refinance, organized so the file moves through underwriting without repeated requests. When the property is in a Midlands flood zone, we also note the flood insurance question early, since the premium can change whether the DSCR calculation works at all.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Columbia, SC | Genstone

rental-renovation.intro: In Columbia, the rental that runs well is the one that stays cool, dry and termite-free. Heat, humidity and pests generate more work orders here than almost anything else, and a renovation that ignores them leads to expensive service calls and unhappy tenants. Genstone Construction renovates single-family rentals across Columbia and the Midlands for individual landlords, funds, REITs and other portfolio owners. We handle acquisition rehabs, turns between tenants and deferred maintenance through vetted, licensed South Carolina contractors managed by a designated field manager. Progress shows up as photos and milestones, and nothing is paid until the matching work is done. Most of our Columbia rental work covers post-war ranches in North Columbia, Eau Claire, Dentsville and St. Andrews, along with older houses near USC and mill cottages in Olympia. Each house gets a scope built for how it was constructed.

sections.body:
A Columbia rental portfolio might include a mill house in Olympia, a 1950s ranch in Eau Claire and a 1990s house in Northeast Columbia. Each rents to a different tenant pool and fails differently. In Olympia, the budget goes under the floor and into every wire and pipe. The ranch needs HVAC and ductwork, electrical upgrades and plumbing replacement. The newer house mostly needs roof, HVAC and water heater replacements, and possibly polybutylene repiping.

We set portfolio specifications for visible and replaceable items, including flooring, paint colors, fixtures, appliances and hardware, so maintenance teams stock fewer parts and tenants see consistent quality. Each property then gets a scope built around its era and construction. When a project is complete, we record system ages and equipment details in the property file, which gives your property manager a real baseline for capital planning. In a climate where HVAC failures are urgent, knowing which systems are oldest helps you plan replacements before they fail mid-summer.

sections.h2: Cutting HVAC, moisture and termite calls
sections.body:
Three issues drive the bulk of rental calls in Columbia: air conditioning that can't keep up, moisture in bathrooms and crawlspaces, and termites. A rental renovation that addresses them pays back every year.

We size heat pumps correctly for each house, seal or replace leaky ductwork, add return air where needed and make sure condensate lines drain properly. Bathrooms get exterior-vented fans and surrounds that don't leak. Crawlspaces get vapor barriers, sealed ducts and drainage corrections. Termite treatment with a renewable bond protects framing, and we correct the conditions that attract termites, such as wood touching soil, leaking gutters and downspouts discharging against the foundation. Inside, durable flooring, scrubbable paint and solid counters survive tenant turnover. These choices don't change a listing photo much, but they change what the property costs to own. In Columbia, a heat pump that quits in August is not a routine work order; it's an emergency that can lose you a tenant. Treating cooling capacity, duct sealing and termite protection as core rental infrastructure, rather than optional upgrades, is the most reliable way to keep a Midlands rental profitable through repeated summers.

Columbia's rental calendar has busy periods tied to the USC academic year and military moves at Fort Jackson, and turns during those periods need to move quickly. Genstone Construction handles make-ready work across the Midlands, and our sister company Genstone Field Services supports portfolio owners with inspections, occupied maintenance, turns and code compliance. A typical turn includes paint, flooring repair or replacement, fixture and appliance checks, cleaning and repair of tenant damage.

We photograph conditions at the start of each turn for deposit decisions. When a turn uncovers a bigger issue, like termite damage behind a baseboard, a soft floor near a tub or a failing HVAC system, we document it and price it separately so you can decide whether to address it now or plan it for later. Each turn is paid after completion, and our one-year workmanship warranty covers the repairs but not tenant damage or normal wear. Portfolio owners can pre-approve standard turn pricing so routine Columbia make-ready work starts the day keys come back.

faqs.q: Do you work with institutional rental owners in Columbia?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone works with individual landlords, investment funds, REITs, mortgage servicers and banks. For portfolio owners in Columbia we standardize specifications, turn pricing and reporting across properties. Even so, each Columbia house keeps a separate scope, budget and file under its own field manager. Owners with houses split between Columbia, West Columbia, Cayce and Irmo can use one specification and reporting format across all of them, which makes comparing turn costs and system ages between properties far simpler.

faqs.q: Can you prepare student rentals near USC between leases?
faqs.a: Yes. Student leases near USC often end together, which creates a short window for turns and renovations. We plan scopes in advance, order materials early and schedule trades so work starts as soon as tenants move out. That shortens vacancy during the busiest part of the Columbia rental calendar. For portfolio owners with several houses near campus, we can stagger crews so each property turns in sequence rather than competing for the same trades in the same week.

faqs.q: Can you replace HVAC in an occupied Columbia rental?
faqs.a: Yes. HVAC replacement is one of the most common occupied jobs we do in Columbia, often on an urgent basis during summer. We coordinate access and timing through your property manager to keep tenant disruption short. Genstone Field Services also handles other occupied maintenance and inspections for portfolio owners. Where the ductwork is the real problem, we may recommend a temporary repair and scheduling the full duct replacement for the next vacancy, so the tenant isn't displaced during peak heat.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovation in Columbia, SC | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Duplex and small multifamily renovation in Columbia, SC: student-area buildings near USC, divided older houses and suburban fourplexes, phased for tenants.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Columbia
multifamily-renovation.intro: Columbia's small multifamily stock follows its rental demand. Near USC and Five Points, duplexes, triplexes and small apartment buildings house students and young professionals. In older neighborhoods like Shandon, Elmwood Park and Cottontown, some larger houses were divided into apartments decades ago. And across Dentsville, St. Andrews and other suburban areas, 1970s and 1980s duplexes and fourplexes rent to working families and military households. Genstone Construction renovates those properties for investors who need shared systems upgraded, units modernized, tenants managed during construction and permits handled properly. A designated field manager coordinates licensed South Carolina trades, and draws are tied to completed work. Termite damage and crawlspace moisture show up in nearly every older Columbia building we evaluate, so they're priced up front rather than discovered mid-project.

sections.h2: Student-area buildings near USC and Five Points
sections.body:
Duplexes and small buildings in Shandon, Rosewood, Olympia, Granby and the Five Points area see heavy use and frequent turnover. Common problems include worn flooring, damaged doors and walls, aging HVAC systems in every unit, plumbing patched many times and exterior stairs or porches with rot where they meet the building. Termite damage and crawlspace moisture are frequent findings as well.

We renovate these buildings to handle years of student use. Hard-surface flooring replaces carpet, solid-core doors replace hollow ones, kitchens get durable counters and cabinets, and bathrooms get one-piece surrounds and exterior-vented fans. Heat pumps are sized for each unit with filters tenants can reach. Exterior stairs and porches are rebuilt with proper flashing and hardware. Summer, when many student leases end, is the natural window for heavier work, so we plan scopes in spring and order materials early. Check Columbia's occupancy limits for unrelated tenants before adding bedrooms.

sections.h2: Divided houses in Columbia's older neighborhoods
sections.body:
Larger houses in Elmwood Park, Cottontown, Shandon and Waverly were sometimes divided into two to four apartments, often with minimal attention to fire separation or independent systems. Typical findings include a single electrical service split into subpanels, shared plumbing stacks, exterior stairs added to reach upper units and smoke alarm coverage that doesn't meet current standards. Some conversions were never approved, so confirming the legal unit count with the city before purchase is essential.

Renovating these buildings starts with life safety and shared systems: separate HVAC for each unit, upgraded electrical service with separate panels and meters, fire-rated separation between units, interconnected smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and code-compliant egress. Exterior changes in protected districts like Elmwood Park or Cottontown need design review. Unit interiors follow, often using one finished unit as the model for the rest of the building. On these older Columbia buildings, termite and moisture damage under shared floors often turns up once the units are opened, so we price likely repairs before the work begins.

The 1970s and 1980s duplexes and fourplexes in Dentsville, St. Andrews, Irmo and other suburban areas were built as multifamily from the start. They usually have simple, repeated floor plans, slab or crawlspace foundations and shared roofs. Construction is generally sound, but original systems are failing together: HVAC equipment, water heaters, early electrical panels, single-pane windows and sometimes polybutylene supply lines.

Repeated layouts make renovation efficient, since the first unit's scope applies to the rest and materials can be ordered in bulk. We start with shared items such as roof, water service, sewer lines and exterior repairs, then renovate units together if the building is vacant or one at a time if tenants remain. Work affecting occupied units is scheduled with notice through your property manager, and fire separation and alarms are maintained throughout. Draws follow completed units, so capital tracks progress. Fourplexes near Fort Jackson Boulevard and Decker Boulevard often turn over with military moves, which can open units for renovation sooner than lease dates suggest.

faqs.q: When should I schedule a renovation near USC?
faqs.a: Summer usually works out, because many student leases end at the same time and heavy interior work won't disrupt occupied units. We plan scopes in spring, order materials early and schedule trades to fit the gap between move-out and move-in. Shared exterior work can sometimes happen during the school year with tenants in place. Ordering HVAC equipment early matters most, since summer is also when Columbia's heating and cooling contractors are busiest.

faqs.q: How do you handle a divided house that may not be legal?
faqs.a: We recommend confirming the legal unit count with the City of Columbia before purchase. If the units are legal, the renovation focuses on life safety and independent systems. If not, the building may need to be reduced in units or go through approval, which changes the investment entirely. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review can identify the major costs either way. We can walk the building with you beforehand.

faqs.q: Can I use FHA 203(k) to buy a Columbia duplex?
faqs.a: Yes. The FHA 203(k) program covers one- to four-unit properties when the buyer lives in one unit, which makes it an option for owner-occupant investors buying an older Columbia duplex or divided house. As a certified 203(k) contractor, Genstone prepares the bids and draw paperwork the lender asks for. Buyers sometimes use the program on a divided house in Elmwood Park or Cottontown, living in one unit while rent from the others helps carry the mortgage. Your lender can confirm current program rules.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Columbia, SC | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Columbia, SC: itemized bids, consultant coordination and draws for Limited and Standard loans on Midlands houses.
fha-203k.intro: Many Columbia houses fail a standard FHA appraisal for reasons that are fixable: a worn-out roof, dead air conditioning in a climate where it's essential, termite damage, peeling paint on a pre-1978 house or unsafe wiring. The FHA 203(k) loan lets buyers purchase those houses and finance the repairs in a single mortgage. Our firm is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor. We work with Columbia homebuyers, agents, renovation lenders and HUD consultants to prepare the itemized bids and draw documentation the program requires, then complete the work with a designated field manager and licensed South Carolina trades. Many of the Columbia houses that fit most often are post-war ranches and older bungalows in established neighborhoods.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard 203(k) for a Columbia house
sections.body:
Columbia buyers whose houses need mostly non-structural work can use the Limited 203(k), which finances up to $75,000 without a HUD consultant. For many Columbia ranches and bungalows, that covers a roof, heat pump and ductwork, an electrical panel upgrade, a PEX repipe, windows, kitchen and bath updates, flooring and lead-safe paint work. Termite treatment and minor repairs can fit too, depending on the extent of damage.

The Standard 203(k) is for structural repairs and larger projects, with a $5,000 minimum repair amount and a HUD consultant who prepares the work write-up and inspects draws. In Columbia, Standard loans are common on mill houses in Olympia and Granby that need pier and floor framing work, older houses with significant termite damage, flood-affected properties needing major repair and projects that reconfigure the floor plan. We assess the house during the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review and tell you which program it likely fits. If the house has a recorded flood history, we discuss that with the lender at the start, since it can affect both the scope and the insurance requirements on the loan.

sections.h2: Columbia houses that fit the 203(k) program
sections.body:
In Columbia, the 203(k) fits most naturally where the price is low enough to leave room for repairs and the finished value still covers the whole loan. That often describes ranches in North Columbia, Eau Claire, Hollywood-Rose Hill, Dentsville and St. Andrews, older houses in Waverly and Cottontown, unrenovated mill houses in Olympia and Granby, and some properties in West Columbia and Cayce.

Agents in Columbia often turn to the 203(k) when an FHA appraisal calls for repairs the seller won't make: a roof near the end of its life, inoperable HVAC, chipping paint, missing handrails, termite damage or electrical hazards. Instead of losing the sale, the buyer can finance the repairs. Because the program covers one- to four-unit properties with an owner-occupant, it also works for duplexes near USC and in older neighborhoods. Homes in protected historic districts qualify, but exterior work needs design review, which we build into the schedule. For buyers who want to live near USC, downtown or Five Points but can't afford a finished renovation, the program can be a realistic route into an older house there.

sections.h2: Bids, consultants and draws in the Midlands
sections.body:
Renovation lenders need an itemized bid from a licensed contractor, and on Standard loans the bid must match the consultant's work write-up. Genstone's estimators prepare detailed bids with labor and materials by line item and work with the HUD consultant to resolve differences before underwriting.

Draw requests go in as stages are finished; on Standard loans the consultant checks the work before the lender releases money. The City of Columbia, Richland County or the appropriate Lexington County jurisdiction issues permits and performs code inspections, and the final inspection needs to be complete before the last draw. We manage permits, inspections, the CL-100 and lien waivers from every trade. Buyers and agents see progress through photos and milestones, and final payment follows the homeowner's approval. Because Columbia summers are hard on unconditioned houses, we usually schedule HVAC installation early in the project so other trades can work in a cooler house, which tends to keep the rest of the schedule moving. If the house sits in a protected district such as Elmwood Park or Cottontown, design review for exterior work is filed at the start so it doesn't hold up the final draw.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) cover termite damage in Columbia?
faqs.a: Yes. Both treatment and framing repair can be financed. Minor damage may fit within the Limited 203(k), while extensive structural damage typically requires the Standard program and a HUD consultant. Hidden damage is common in older Columbia houses, so the contingency reserve is important. We assess visible damage during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and coordinate the CL-100 with a licensed pest control company, so the lender has the documentation it needs at closing.

faqs.q: Do Columbia 203(k) buyers need to move out during renovation?
faqs.a: On most projects, yes, because kitchens, baths or HVAC are out of service, and Columbia summers make a house without air conditioning hard to live in. Some lenders allow mortgage payments during part of the renovation period to be included in the loan. We give a realistic schedule with the bid. Smaller Limited projects, especially ones that keep the existing air conditioning running, sometimes allow the buyer to move in sooner.

faqs.q: What if the renovation uncovers more damage?
faqs.a: 203(k) loans include a contingency reserve for this. Older Columbia houses sometimes reveal termite damage, rotted framing or old wiring once walls and floors are opened. We document the finding with photos, price the repair and submit a change order through the lender, and the consultant on Standard loans, before any additional work. The buyer sees the photos and approves the cost before anything changes in the scope.

reo-renovation.title: REO and Bank-Owned Renovation in Columbia, SC | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO and bank-owned property renovation in Columbia, SC for servicers, banks, funds and GSEs: securing, drying and repairing vacant Midlands homes.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Columbia
reo-renovation.intro: Columbia's heat is unforgiving to a vacant house. A summer without air conditioning can turn a sound property into one with mold on every wall, and termites keep working whether or not anyone is watching. Servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders send us their Midlands properties, and Government-Sponsored Enterprises count Genstone among their preferred contractors. Across Columbia and the Midlands, we coordinate vetted, licensed South Carolina contractors managed by a Genstone field manager who produces the documentation asset managers require: itemized bids, photo documentation, permit records, inspection results and lien waivers from every trade. Our executive team's REO background shapes how we secure, scope and report on bank-owned properties.

sections.h2: What vacant Columbia houses look like
sections.body:
Mold is the most common problem in vacant Columbia houses. With power off or the HVAC disabled, humidity builds through the long summer and mold spreads on drywall, cabinets, ceilings and furnishings. Roof leaks and plumbing failures make it much worse. Crawlspaces collect moisture, floors cup and termites continue to damage framing.

Theft and vandalism are also common. HVAC condensers, copper and appliances are frequent targets, and broken windows or doors invite trespassers. Overgrown yards and debris draw complaints quickly. Properties near Gills Creek and the rivers may carry flood damage from 2015 or later storms that was never fully repaired. A Columbia REO scope usually starts with securing the house, stopping water intrusion and treating termites, then moves to mold remediation, system replacement and repairs needed to make the property marketable or financeable. Our first visit focuses on stopping further loss, with dehumidification and power restoration requested where the client allows it, because each additional humid week adds to the remediation cost.

sections.h2: Code enforcement and permits on Columbia REO
sections.body:
The City of Columbia's code enforcement staff handle minimum housing standards, overgrown lots, debris and vacant or unsafe structures. Vacant properties draw complaints quickly in residential neighborhoods, and open cases can complicate a sale. Cited violations come first; each correction is photographed and the re-inspection is scheduled.

Renovation work requiring permits goes through the City of Columbia's building inspections staff, Richland County Building Codes and Inspections or the appropriate Lexington County jurisdiction. Properties in FEMA flood hazard areas may face floodplain review when repairs are substantial, and bank-owned houses in protected historic districts need design review for exterior changes. For REO clients we keep permit records, inspection results, the CL-100 and lien waivers in the property file. Genstone Field Services can handle property preservation, inspections and code compliance alongside renovation, keeping one consistent record from first visit to sale. That continuity matters when a buyer's attorney or lender asks for proof that a cited violation was corrected.

sections.h2: Choosing the right REO scope in Columbia
sections.body:
The right budget for a Columbia REO comes down to the street it's on and who is likely to buy it. In Shandon, Rosewood, Melrose Heights, Wales Garden and other neighborhoods with strong owner-occupant demand, buyers compare listings to renovated houses, so a fuller renovation can significantly improve recovery. In areas where investors make up more of the buyer pool, a repair-to-market scope that brings the house to financeable condition is often the better choice.

A Columbia repair-to-market scope typically includes a sound roof, working HVAC, functional plumbing and electrical, termite treatment and repair with a clean CL-100, mold remediation, safety items like handrails and smoke alarms and lead-safe paint correction on pre-1978 houses. When the right path isn't obvious, the asset manager gets both scopes side by side, itemized and photographed in the client's format. Near USC, an unrenovated bank-owned house may also draw strong interest from investors planning student rentals, which is worth weighing before committing to a full renovation. Each bid reflects the conditions documented at our walkthrough, including termite and crawlspace findings that a drive-by valuation can't capture.

faqs.q: Does Genstone handle GSE-owned properties in Columbia?
faqs.a: Yes. Government-Sponsored Enterprises list Genstone as a preferred contractor, and we also take Midlands assignments from servicers, banks and other lenders. We follow their bid formats, coordinate licensed South Carolina trades and keep photos, permit records and lien waivers with each Columbia property file. A designated field manager is the single point of contact for each address, from the first securing visit through the final listing photos, so the asset manager always knows who to call about a given property.

faqs.q: How do you handle mold in a vacant Columbia house?
faqs.a: We identify the moisture source first, whether a roof leak, plumbing failure, disabled HVAC or crawlspace moisture. Affected materials are removed, the cause is corrected and the area is documented before and after for the asset manager. Larger mold problems are handled by a licensed remediation specialist coordinated within the same project. In Columbia's climate, restoring power and running dehumidification early can limit how far the mold spreads before remediation begins.

faqs.q: Can you handle flood-damaged REO near Gills Creek?
faqs.a: Yes. Flood-damaged properties need careful documentation, removal of affected materials, drying and mold remediation before rebuilding. If the property is in a FEMA flood hazard area and damage is substantial, floodplain rules may affect the repair approach, which we review with the asset manager before finalizing the scope. We document the flood damage thoroughly with photos, since buyers, insurers and lenders will ask about the property's history when it comes to market.
